plan.contextChunk: This figure looks straight down the axis of a chair-form cyclohexane ring in two matched models that color-code the two kinds of hydrogen position. On the left is a space-filling model: a compact dark gray core of ring carbons is surrounded by six large red spheres and six large blue spheres packed against one another, the red ones sitting toward the center of the disc and the blue ones fanning outward around the rim, the two colors alternating as the eye travels around the ring. A magenta arrow at the upper left points to a red sphere and is labeled "Axial"; a blue arrow at the top points to a blue sphere and is labeled "Equatorial". On the right the same view appears as a ball-and-stick model, the six dark gray carbons forming a hexagonal outline, with red spheres projecting from alternating carbons and blue spheres held outward from every carbon on thin pale rods. Separating the two positions by color rather than by perspective lets the reader count them directly, establishing that each ring carbon bears exactly one axial and one equatorial hydrogen and that each face carries three of each in alternating order.

Space-filling model (left): 6 axial hydrogens (red, large overlapping spheres)
Space-filling model (left): 6 equatorial hydrogens (blue, large overlapping spheres)
Ball-and-stick model (right): 6 ring carbons (dark gray, small separated spheres)
Ball-and-stick model (right): 6 axial hydrogens (red, small separated spheres)
Ball-and-stick model (right): 6 equatorial hydrogens (blue, small separated spheres)
Ball-and-stick model (right): 18 connecting bonds (light gray cylinders)
Text label 'Equatorial' with an arrow pointing to a blue hydrogen on the left model
Text label 'Axial' with an arrow pointing to a red hydrogen on the left model

interactions.teaches: Rotating the scene away from the top-down view reveals the 3D chair puckering and shows the 3 downward-pointing axial hydrogens hidden beneath the ring.
Selecting any ring carbon highlights its paired axial and equatorial hydrogens together, clarifying that the two positions coexist on every carbon.

demo_steps.title: Top-down view of both positions
demo_steps.narration: Viewed from above, the carbons form a hexagon. Equatorial hydrogens fan outward around the perimeter, while axial hydrogens point directly at or away from us.

demo_steps.title: Isolate axial hydrogens
demo_steps.narration: Filtering to just the red axial hydrogens shows that they alternate pointing straight up and straight down around the ring.

demo_steps.title: Isolate equatorial hydrogens

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Two models placed side-by-side: space-filling center at x = -3.5, ball-and-stick center at x = +3.5. Y is the vertical axis. The average plane of both rings is the XZ plane. Vertices of the hexagon from top-down sit at 12, 2, 4, 6, 8, and 10 o'clock. Standard cyclohexane chair coordinates (C-C distance ~1.54 units, puckered alternating ±0.25 units in Y). Axial bonds point straight up (+Y) or straight down (-Y) on alternating carbons. Equatorial bonds tilt slightly counter to their carbon's axial direction and extend outward. Colors: Carbons dark gray #444444, Axial H red #de4231, Equatorial H blue #3ea0e6, 'Axial' label/arrow magenta #c92275, 'Equatorial' label/arrow teal #3e7b8f. Sizes: Space-filling uses C radius 1.2, H radius 0.9. Ball-and-stick uses C radius 0.4, H radius 0.25, bond radius 0.08.
interactionPlan.notes: For the click interaction on the ball-and-stick model, dim all unselected atoms and bonds to 0.3 opacity to make the selected C, its 2 H's, and their bonds stand out. For the toggle interaction, transition the opacity of the hidden hydrogen group (and their connecting bonds in the right model) to 0, keeping the carbon skeletons fully visible. Ensure the arrows for the labels dynamically follow their target spheres if the user orbits.

authoredContext:
As shown in the figure, each carbon atom in chair cyclohexane has one axial and one equatorial hydrogen. Furthermore, each side of the ring has three axial and three equatorial hydrogens in an alternating arrangement. For example, if the top side of the ring has axial hydrogens on carbons 1, 3, and 5, then it has equatorial hydrogens on carbons 2, 4, and 6. The reverse is true for the bottom side: carbons 1, 3, and 5 have equatorial hydrogens, but carbons 2, 4, and 6 have axial hydrogens (the figure).

Alternating axial and equatorial positions in chair cyclohexane, looking directly down the ring axis. Each carbon atom has one axial and one equatorial position, and each face has alternating axial and equatorial positions.

The space-filling model and ball and stick model of cyclohexane with alternate axial and equatorial positions, represented by red and blue spheres, respectively.

Note that we haven’t used the words cis and trans in this discussion of cyclohexane conformation. Two hydrogens on the same side of the ring are always cis, regardless of whether they’re axial or equatorial and regardless of whether they’re adjacent. Similarly, two hydrogens on opposite sides of the ring are always trans.
